title: State Architecture Patterns: Designing a Scalable React State Strategy
description: Design a comprehensive state architecture for enterprise React applications: separating UI state, client domain state, server state, and form state with clear boundaries, colocation principles, and the Zustand pattern for mid-complexity applications.

data.text: The State Taxonomy: Four Categories with Clear Boundaries

The most common React architecture mistake is using a single, undifferentiated global store for all state categories. This creates coupling that slows every developer who touches the application: UI state (dropdown open/closed) shares the same update cycle as server state (conversation list freshness), which couples to form state (active search query). A mature state architecture defines four distinct categories, each with its own dedicated management tool, ownership boundary, and invalidation strategy.

data.text: State should live as close to where it is used as possible. This prevents unnecessary global state pollution. If only one component needs a piece of state, it should own it locally. If two sibling components share state, lift it to their closest common ancestor. If state is needed across many distant components, then and only then, move it to a global store.

data.title: Zustand Store for Mid-Complexity Client Domain State
data.content: Zustand provides a lightweight alternative to Redux Toolkit for client domain state that doesn't need action creators, reducers, or DevTools time-travel—just simple, typed reactive state.

data.title: The Redux vs Zustand Decision
data.content: Use Redux Toolkit when you need: (1) time-travel debugging with DevTools, (2) complex cross-slice derived state, (3) middleware (RTK Query, logging), or (4) a large team that benefits from strict action-based constraints. Use Zustand when you need lightweight reactive client state without boilerplate—typically for UI state that needs to be accessed by many unrelated components.

data.title: State Architecture Review Checklist
items: Every piece of state is categorized into one of the four buckets before choosing a tool
No server-fetched data is stored in Zustand or Redux—TanStack Query owns all remote state
UI ephemeral state (dropdowns, modals, hover) stays local to the component that owns it
Conversation and document IDs passed via URL params so pages are shareable and browser-back-compatible
Zustand selectors use shallow equality comparison to prevent unnecessary consumer re-renders
State architecture documented as an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) for the team

data.title: Summary & Phase 2 Conclusion
points: The four state categories (UI, Client Domain, Server, Form) each deserve their own tool and boundary.
Colocation keeps state as local as possible, only globalizing when genuinely needed.
Zustand provides a lightweight, boilerplate-free alternative to RTK for client domain state.
Phase 2 is complete: you have mastered advanced React patterns, TypeScript, and state architecture.
data.takeaway: A great state architecture is invisible to users and obvious to developers: every state category lives in the right tool with clear ownership, preventing both over-engineering and tangled coupling.
